article.overview:
A neutron-based hydrogen detector looks for hydrogen in the uppermost layer of a planetary surface by measuring neutrons. Hydrogen matters on the Moon because hydrogen in the cold polar regions may indicate water ice. The method does not see hydrogen directly. It measures how the flux and energy of neutrons leaving the ground change, because hydrogen-rich material alters the neutron population that reaches a detector in orbit [1][2].

Scope of this article. This article covers neutron spectrometers designed to detect hydrogen by measuring neutrons, with lunar-orbit examples.

- In scope: the neutron measurement chain, its energy bands, and the two documented lunar-orbit examples.
- Out of scope: gamma-ray spectrometers (catalogue 57), which measure a different radiation signal; the generic neutron spectrometer entry (catalogue 58), which is not duplicated here; and other hydrogen and water detectors (catalogue 99, 100 and 103), which are not covered by this article.

Status summary. The article distinguishes three kinds of evidence:

- Flown in lunar orbit (historical): the Lunar Prospector Neutron Spectrometer (NS), January 1998 to July 1999 [4][7].
- Flown in lunar orbit (LRO): the Lunar Exploration Neutron Detector (LEND), described in its PDS documentation [2][3], in a 2010 instrument paper that reports design and calibration plans rather than measured results [1], and in a 2021 calibration study of its observations [9].
- Planetary heritage (Mars, not lunar): HEND on Mars Odyssey, named in the LEND documentation as LEND's predecessor [2].
article.description:
The LEND instrument, as documented in its PDS software interface specification [2], comprises four parts:

1. Eight helium-3 (3He) sensors for thermal and epithermal neutrons. Four are uncollimated (STN1–3 and SETN) and four are collimated (CSETN1–4). The 2021 calibration study also describes LEND as having eight helium-3 detectors [9].
2. A collimating module that defines the instrument's field of view. It uses external polyethylene for moderation and internal boron-10 (10B) layers for absorption, and absorbs most neutrons arriving from outside its field of view [2].
3. Cadmium shields on the collimated sensors, which absorb neutrons below about 0.4 eV, mainly thermal neutrons [2].
4. SHEN, a stilbene scintillator for high-energy neutrons, with 16 energy channels from 300 keV to more than 15 MeV and a 40° field of view (half width at half maximum) [2].

The LEND product columns define the following neutron energy bands [2]:

| Band | Energy range | Product column |
|---|---|---|
| Thermal | below 0.4 eV | THERMAL |
| Epithermal 1 | 0.4 eV to 100 eV | EPITHERMAL_FLUX1 |
| Epithermal 2 | 0.10 keV to 10 keV | EPITHERMAL_FLUX2 |
| Epithermal 3 | 10 keV to 1.0 MeV | EPITHERMAL_FLUX3 |
| Fast 1 | 1 MeV to 2.5 MeV | FAST_FLUX1 |
| Fast 2 | 2.5 MeV to 7.5 MeV | FAST_FLUX2 |
| Fast 3 | 7.5 MeV to 10 MeV | FAST_FLUX3 |

The specification prints the Epithermal 2 range as "1 0 keV", which appears to be a formatting error for 10 keV [2]. The THERMAL column is described in the specification as epithermal, but its stated range is thermal; this article uses the range [2].

The Lunar Prospector Neutron Spectrometer is described in NASA's mission text as having detected hydrogen at the lunar poles, which NASA assumed to be in the form of water [4]. Its two helium-3 counters, mass and power are documented in the PDS instrument catalogue entry [7] (see Physical Specifications).
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
- Hydrogen mapping of the uppermost surface. Mitrofanov et al. describe LEND as optimized for "high spatial resolution hydrogen mapping of the Moon's upper-most surface" [1].
- Near-surface water ice in polar cold traps. LEND's stated goals include identifying possible near-surface water ice in polar cold traps [1]. The PDS instrument context page lists a hydrogen sensitivity of 100 ppm as an objective [3].
- Shadowed polar craters. Spaceflight Now's description of the LRO mission states that LEND "will be able to detect hydrogen in permanently shadowed craters near the lunar poles that may be water ice" [6].
- Radiation environment. Mitrofanov et al. list characterizing the radiation environment in lunar orbit, relevant to humans, as one of LEND's requirements [1].
- Historical polar water-ice estimate. NASA's Lunar Prospector page gives "possibly about" 330 million short tons (300 million metric tons) of water ice mixed into the regolith at each pole [4]. This is an estimate from the mission team's interpretation, not a direct measurement of ice quantity.
article.operating_principle:
Neutrons are produced in the lunar regolith when high-energy particles strike the surface, and some of them escape. This is general background and is not supported by a cited source in this article (see Limitations, Uncertainties and Evidence Gaps). Collisions with hydrogen slow neutrons down. Where hydrogen-rich material is present near the surface, the population of lower-energy (epithermal) neutrons leaving the ground changes, and an orbiting detector can record that change in energy bands.

LEND measures this with its eight 3He sensors, which detect thermal and epithermal neutrons [2]. Cadmium shields and the collimator restrict which neutrons each collimated sensor sees [2]. The collimated system provides a horizontal resolution of 5 km for LRO at an altitude of 50 km [2]. Fast neutrons are measured separately by the SHEN scintillator across its energy channels [2].

The Lunar Prospector NS used two identical helium-3 gas proportional counters, one covered with cadmium and one with tin, so that the two sensors respond to different neutron energy ranges [7].

The averaged LEND map products use grid cells of 0.5° × 0.5° at the poles and 1.0° × 1.0° at the equator [2]. These are data-product grids, not the instrument's resolution.
article.scientific_importance:
Orbital hydrogen mapping is important because the Moon's polar cold traps are permanently shadowed areas where volatile material could survive over long periods. Neutron measurements sample hydrogen in the upper metre or so of the surface, a depth that optical instruments cannot see. NASA's mission page for Lunar Prospector describes the polar hydrogen result as the first direct evidence of water ice at the lunar poles [4]. The original polar interpretation was published by Feldman et al. in *Science* in 1998 [8].

The hydrogen signal does not identify the chemical form of the hydrogen. NASA's Lunar Prospector interpretation assumed water [4], and LEND's objectives describe testing for water ice in cold traps rather than proving it [1]. The LEND data are also intended to inform the next stages of global lunar exploration and to support studies of hydrogen implantation and diffusion in regolith [1].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a neutron-based hydrogen detector. The two lunar-orbit examples below use different periods, sensor architectures and levels of documentation. Where values are given, they describe different missions and measurement designs and should not be compared as though they came from one instrument. The Lunar Prospector values are from the PDS instrument catalogue [7]. The LEND mass and power are from a secondary mission summary [6] and have not been confirmed against a primary instrument record.

examples.power_source_note: Value from the PDS instrument catalogue entry (NSINST.CAT), which gives 2.5 W.
examples.sensor_configuration: Two identical helium-3 filled gas proportional counters. The other has a 0.75 mm tin shield, which the catalogue describes as sensitive to thermal and epithermal neutrons.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
LEND operates in lunar orbit, and its resolution figure is quoted at 50 km altitude [2]. The Lunar Prospector NS was operated at about 40 km during its lower-orbit phase, for higher-resolution studies [4]. Orbital altitude therefore directly sets the footprint and resolution of any neutron map.

LEND's measurement modes and data volume are documented [2]. The specification also divides the sensors into uncollimated and collimated groups [2]; the sources fetched do not explain the purpose of the uncollimated group. Thermal control, radiation exposure and vacuum operation are general engineering constraints for any orbiting instrument. No thermal, radiation or vacuum qualification values were retrieved for either example, so none is stated here.
article.limitations:
- Coarse spatial resolution. The LEND collimated system resolves about 5 km horizontally at 50 km altitude according to the PDS specification [2]. Spaceflight Now gives 10 km [6]. Either way, individual small hydrogen sources cannot be separated at that scale.
- Depth averaging. Spaceflight Now's description of LEND gives a sensing depth of "down to ~1 meter" [6]. A neutron signal integrates over that depth and cannot show how hydrogen is layered within it.
- Hydrogen is not the same as water. Neutron measurements respond to hydrogen content, not chemical form. NASA's Lunar Prospector interpretation assumed water [4].
- Estimates depend on models. The Lunar Prospector water-ice amount is given as "possibly about" a value, and is an interpretation of the neutron data [4].
- Incomplete or unconfirmed instrument specifications. The Lunar Prospector NS values come from the PDS catalogue [7]. The LEND mass and power come from a single secondary source [6]. LEND dimensions and HEND specifications are not available in the sources accessed.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Both documented lunar examples are orbital payloads. They do not describe a surface deployment, so the discussion below covers orbiter integration and operations.
transportation_process: Integrate the detector assembly with a host orbiter, including its power, data and thermal interfaces.
Launch the spacecraft, carry out cruise and insert it into lunar orbit.
Commission the instrument, set it to measurement mode and downlink its data.
Operate the instrument in lunar orbit, with any orbit changes the mission requires.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not applicable to either documented lunar example, which are orbital payloads. No surface deployment mechanism is described in the sources accessed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Lunar Prospector Neutron Spectrometer (1998-1999) and LEND on LRO are the two documented lunar-orbit examples. HEND on Mars Odyssey is a planetary heritage example that is not lunar.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander or surface-host compatibility is assessed or claimed. The orbital host for LEND is LRO [2][3]; the orbital host for the Lunar Prospector NS was Lunar Prospector [4]. Host interface details were not retrieved for either.

article.historical_significance:
Lunar Prospector's neutron spectrometer, flown in 1998–1999, provided the polar hydrogen result that NASA presents as the first direct evidence of water ice at the lunar poles [4]. The polar interpretation was published by Feldman et al. in *Science* in 1998 [8]. The full text of that paper was not accessed for this version, so its specific values are not reproduced here. Its successor in the documented lineage is LEND, which the LEND specification describes as a follow-on to HEND on Mars Odyssey [2].

The 2010 Space Science Reviews paper on LEND describes its design for three LRO requirements: hydrogen mapping, near-surface water ice in polar cold traps, and the lunar-orbit radiation environment [1]. The paper reports calibration and planned observations, not measured results [1]. A 2021 arXiv study cross-calibrates LEND observations against Lunar Prospector epithermal-neutron data and other references, and describes a ten-plus-year LEND observation campaign [9].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
This article is a second-revision draft (v2). It closes several v1 gaps: the Lunar Prospector NS mass, power and counter dimensions are now given from the PDS catalogue [7]; the 1998 polar-hydrogen paper is now cited [8]; and a LEND-specific image is now included [10]. The following gaps remain open and affect confidence in the article.
- The full text of Feldman et al. (1998) [8] was not accessed. Its citation comes from bibliographic records, and claims about it are limited to the NASA page [4].
- The LEND mass (25.8 kg) and average power (11.6 W) come from a single secondary mission summary [6] and have not been confirmed against a primary PDS or NASA instrument record. No LEND dimensions were found.
- The LEND horizontal resolution is 5 km in the PDS specification [2] and 10 km in Spaceflight Now [6]. The article reports both and does not reconcile them.
- LEND's launch date, orbit-insertion date and current operating status were not verified.
- The neutron production and moderation physics in the Operating Principle section is general background and is not supported by a cited source.
- The Lunar Prospector NS mass and power are from the PDS catalogue entry, which cites a 1998 Binder et al. specification [7]. That specification was not retrieved.
- The LEND SVS image (Figure 2 and Figure 4) is a data visualization, not a hardware photograph. A NASA archived LEND photo was reported in a search result but was not retrieved, so no LEND hardware image is included.
- Image rights and reuse terms were not verified beyond the credits given on the source pages.
- HEND on Mars Odyssey: specifications were not retrieved. Only its heritage relationship to LEND is cited [2].
- Other national lunar neutron instruments were not surveyed. The article covers only the two lunar-orbit examples.
- No lunar landing-site recommendations or lander compatibility claims are made, consistent with the deferral of location recommendations.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: v2 rerun. v1 files (neutron_based_hydrogen_detector_payload_101.md and .json) are unchanged.

Research budget for v2: 5 web searches and 9 page fetch attempts. Five did not return usable content: arXiv PDF (404), Feldman PDF on lpl.arizona.edu (404), openpolar Feldman record (certificate error), and Springer and science.org DOI (redirected to login or paywall).

Lunar Prospector NS mass (3.9 kg), power (2.5 W) and counter dimensions (5 cm diameter by 20 cm long each) are from the PDS instrument catalogue entry NSINST.CAT, which cites a 1998 Binder et al. specification that was not retrieved.

Feldman et al. (1998), Science 281(5382), 1496-1500, DOI 10.1126/science.281.5382.1496: the bibliographic details come from search metadata and an openpolar record. The full text and abstract were not read, so no specific value from the paper is stated.
LEND mass (25.8 kg) and average power (11.6 W) come from the Spaceflight Now LRO article, a secondary source. The PDS specification and PDS context page do not state them. Treat as unconfirmed.
LEND horizontal resolution: 5 km at 50 km altitude (PDS lend_rdr_sis) versus 10 km spatial resolution (Spaceflight Now). Both reported; not reconciled.
The v1 10 km figure was excluded because it lacked a primary source. In v2 it is attributed to Spaceflight Now and not used as the instrument's resolution.

LEND SVS image (lend.2180_print.jpg): downloaded to scratchpad, 1024x576 JPEG, visually checked. It is a data visualization of LEND count rates, not hardware. The source page gives no caption or alt text for this still.
A NASA archived LEND photo credit (NASA/Debbie McCallum) was reported in a search result but was not retrieved or verified. No LEND hardware image is included.

The 2021 arXiv calibration paper (arXiv:2104.03451) was read as an abstract only. The v2 abstract page returned no full text or instrument specifications. Its statements in this article are limited to the abstract (eight helium-3 detectors; ten-plus-year campaign; cross-calibration against Lunar Prospector epithermal-neutron data).
The LRO launch date and LEND activation date were not verified. The Spaceflight Now article does not state them.
The neutron production and moderation physics in the Operating Principle section is general background and is not supported by a cited source.
HEND on Mars Odyssey: no specifications retrieved; the heritage relationship is cited from the LEND specification only.

Images: three JPEG assets were downloaded and confirmed (Lunar Prospector artist's concept; LEND SVS count-rate visualization; LRO spacecraft rendering). Rights and reuse terms were not verified beyond source-page credits.
All JSON URLs were cleaned of query strings and fragments.
Lunar landing-site recommendations and lander compatibility are not included, consistent with the user's deferral. No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is claimed.
